title: The tower, Sodom and the cleansing fire
source_text: Οὐκ οἶδα δ᾿ ὅπως παραπλησίως τῷ κατακλυσμῷ καθήραντι τὴν γῆν, ὡς ὁ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν βούλεται λόγος, οἴεται καὶ τὴν τοῦ πύργου κατάῤῥιψιν γεγονέναι. ἵνα γὰρ μηδὲν αἰνίσσηται ἡ κατὰ τὸν πύργον ἱστορία κειμένη ἐν τῇ Γενέσει ἀλλ᾿, ὡς οἴεται Κέλσος, σαφὴς τυγχάνῃ, οὐ δ᾿ οὕτως φαίνεται ἐπὶ καθαρσίῳ τῆς γῆς τοῦτο συμβεβηκέναι· εἰ μὴ ἄρα καθάρσιον τῆς γῆς οἴεται τὴν καλουμένην τῶν γλωσσῶν „σύγχυσιν“· περὶ ἧς ὁ δυνάμενος εὐκαιρότερον διηγήσεται, ἐπὰν τὸ προκείμενον ᾖ παραστῆσαι καὶ τὰ τῆς κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἱστορίας, τίνα ἔχοι λόγον, καὶ τὰ τῆς περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀναγωγῆς. ἐπεὶ δ᾿ οἴεται Μωϋσέα, τὸν ἀναγράψαντα τὰ περὶ τοῦ πύργου καὶ τῆς τῶν διαλέκτων συγχύσεως, παραφθείροντα τὰ περὶ τῶν Ἀλωέως υἱῶν ἱστορούμενα τοιαῦτα περὶ τοῦ πύργου ἀναγεγραφέναι, λεκτέον ὅτι τὰ μὲν περὶ τῶν Ἀλωέως υἱῶν οὐκ οἶμαι πρὸ Ὁμήρου τινὰ εἰρηκέναι, τὰ δὲ περὶ τοῦ πύργου, πολλῷ πρεσβύτερα Ὁμήρου ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν γραμμάτων εὑρέσεως ὄντα, τὸν Μωϋσέα ἀναγεγραφέναι πείθομαι. τίνες οὖν μᾶλλον τὰ τίνων παραφθείρουσιν; ἆρα τὰ περὶ τοῦ πύργου οἱ περὶ Ἀλωέως υἱῶν ἱστοροῦντες, ἢ τὰ τῶν Ἀλωειδῶν ὁ τὰ περὶ τοῦ πύργου καὶ τῆς συγχύσεως τῶν διαλέκτων γράψας; ἀλλὰ φαίνεται τοῖς ἀδεκάστοις ἀκροαταῖς ἀρχαιότερος Μω(??)σῆς ὢν Ὁμήρου. καὶ τὰ περὶ Σοδόμων δὲ καὶ Γομόῤῥων ὑπὸ Μωϋσέως ἱστορούμενα ἐν τῇ Γενέσει, ὡς διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν πυρὶ ἐξαφανισθέντων. παραβάλλει ὁ Κέλσος τῇ κατὰ τὸν Φαέθοντα ἱστορίᾳ, ἑνὶ σφάλματι. τῷ περὶ τοῦ μὴ τετηρηκέναι τὰ τῆς Μωϋσέως ἀρχαιότητος. ἀκολούθως πάντα ποιήσας. οἱ γὰρ τὰ περὶ Φαέθοντος ἱστοροῦντες ἐοίκασι καὶ Ὁμήρου νεώτεροι, τοῦ πολλῷ Μωϋσέως νεωτέρου. οὐκ ἀρνούμεθα οὖν τὸ καθάρσιον πῦρ καὶ τὴν τοῦ κόσμου φθορὰν ἐπὶ καθαιρέσει τῆς κακίας καὶ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ παντὸς, λέγοντες παρὰ τῶν προφητῶν ἐκ τῶν ἱερῶν βιβλίων μεμαθηκέναι. ἐπὰν μέντοι. ὡς ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν, πολλὰ περὶ μελλόντων οἱ προφῆται λέγοντες ἀποδεικνύωνται περὶ πολλῶν παρεληλυθότων ἠληθευκέναι καὶ δεῖγμα διδόναι τοῦ θεῖον πνεῦμα ἐν αὐτοῖς γεγονέναι, δῆλον ὅτι καὶ περὶ τῶν μελλόντων πιστευτέον αὐτοῖς, μᾶλλον δὲ τῷ ἐν αὐτοῖς θείῳ πνεύματι.
pass_a_gloss: I do not know how (οὐκ οἶδα ὅπως), closely like (παραπλησίως) the flood that purified (καθαίρω) the earth, as the teaching (λόγος) of Jews and Christians wants (βούλεται), he supposes (οἴομαι) the throwing-down (κατάρριψις) of the tower (πύργος) also to have happened. For granted that (ἵνα) the story (ἱστορία) about the tower lying (κεῖμαι) in Genesis hints at / speaks in riddles (αἰνίσσομαι) nothing, but, as Celsus thinks, is clear/plain (σαφής), not even so does this appear to have happened for a purification (καθάρσιον) of the earth; unless perhaps he thinks the so-called 'confusion' (σύγχυσις) of the tongues (γλῶσσαι) a purification of the earth; about which the one who is able will narrate (διηγέομαι) more opportunely (εὐκαιρότερον), when the matter set forth (τὸ προκείμενον) is to present (παρίστημι) both the matters of the story in the passage (κατὰ τὸν τόπον), what sense/account (λόγος) it might have, and the matters of the anagogy/elevated sense (ἀναγωγή) about it. And since he thinks Moses, who recorded (ἀναγράφω) the things about the tower and the confusion of the dialects (διάλεκτοι), corrupting/distorting (παραφθείρω) the things narrated about the sons of Aloeus (Ἀλωεύς), recorded such things about the tower, it must be said that the things about the sons of Aloeus I do not think (οὐκ οἶμαι) anyone said before Homer, but the things about the tower, being much older (πρεσβύτερα) than Homer and even than the invention (εὕρεσις) of Greek letters (γράμματα), I am persuaded (πείθομαι) Moses recorded. Who then rather corrupt whose things? Is it those narrating about the sons of Aloeus who corrupt the things about the tower, or the one who wrote the things about the tower and the confusion of the dialects the things of the Aloadae (Ἀλωεῖδαι)? But to unbribed/impartial (ἀδέκαστος) hearers (ἀκροαταί) Moses appears (φαίνεται) being more ancient (ἀρχαιότερος) than Homer. And the things about Sodom and Gomorrah narrated by Moses in Genesis, as of [cities] made to vanish (ἐξαφανίζω) by fire through (διά) the sin (ἁμαρτία), Celsus compares (παραβάλλω) to the story about Phaethon, having done everything consistently (ἀκολούθως) with one error (σφάλμα), that about not having observed (τηρέω) the matters of the antiquity of Moses. For those narrating about Phaethon seem (ἐοίκασι) to be younger (νεώτεροι) even than Homer, who is much younger than Moses. We do not deny (ἀρνέομαι) therefore the purifying fire (καθάρσιον πῦρ) and the destruction (φθορά) of the world for the taking-down (καθαίρεσις) of wickedness and the renewal (ἀνακαίνωσις) of the whole (τὸ πᾶν), saying we have learned (μανθάνω) it from the prophets (προφῆται) out of the sacred books (ἱερὰ βιβλία). When, however, as we said in the earlier [parts], the prophets, saying many things about things to come (μέλλοντα), are shown (ἀποδείκνυμι) to have spoken truly (ἀληθεύω) about many past things (παρεληλυθότα) and to give a proof (δεῖγμα) of a divine spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) having been in them, it is clear that also about the things to come one must believe (πιστευτέον) them, or rather the divine spirit in them.
pass_b_english: I do not know how he thinks that the overthrow of the tower also took place in the same way as the flood that cleansed the earth, as the teaching of Jews and Christians would have it. For even granting that the story of the tower set down in Genesis (Genesis 11:1–9) speaks in no riddles but, as Celsus thinks, is plain, not even so does it appear that this happened to cleanse the earth; unless, perhaps, he thinks that what is called the “confusion” of tongues (Genesis 11:9) was a cleansing of the earth. Whoever is able will give an account of this at a more suitable time, when the task in hand is to set out both what sense the story in that passage has and what its higher meaning is.

He thinks that Moses, who recorded the events of the tower and the confusion of languages, corrupted the stories told about the sons of Aloeus and so recorded such things about the tower. To this it must be said that I do not think anyone told the stories of the sons of Aloeus before Homer, whereas I am persuaded that Moses recorded the events of the tower, which are much older than Homer and even than the invention of Greek letters. Who, then, is more likely to be corrupting whose stories? Do those who tell of the sons of Aloeus corrupt the events of the tower, or does the man who wrote of the tower and the confusion of languages corrupt the stories of the Aloadae? But to impartial hearers Moses plainly appears to be older than Homer.

Moses also tells in Genesis of Sodom and Gomorrah, how they were wiped out by fire because of their sin (Genesis 19:24–25). Celsus compares this with the story of Phaethon, doing everything in keeping with his one mistake, his failure to take account of the antiquity of Moses. For those who tell of Phaethon seem to be younger even than Homer, and Homer is much younger than Moses.

We do not deny, then, the cleansing fire and the destruction of the world for the removal of wickedness and the renewal of the universe, and we say that we have learned this from the prophets, out of the sacred books. Yet once the prophets, who say many things about the future, are shown, as we said above, to have spoken the truth about many things that are past, and to give proof that the divine Spirit was in them, it is plain that we must believe them about the things to come as well, or rather believe the divine Spirit in them.

choices.choice: 'hints at nothing hidden' to 'speaks in no riddles' (αἰνίσσομαι), dropping the added word 'hidden'
εὐκαιρότερον 'at a more suitable time' (was 'more fittingly'); 'one who is able' to 'Whoever is able'
double question put in the present tense as in the Greek (παραφθείρουσιν)
'a divine Spirit' to 'the divine Spirit' (indefinite article with a capitalised Spirit was misleading)
Genesis 11:1–9, 11:9 (LXX Σύγχυσις) and 19:24–25 checked; note added on the ambiguous ὡς ... λόγος clause

Genesis 11:1–9 does not narrate the tower being thrown down; κατάρριψις is Celsus's view as Origen reports it, and Origen's reply ('not even so does it appear that this happened to cleanse the earth') does not concede it. The clause 'ὡς ὁ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν βούλεται λόγος' can attach either to the flood that cleansed the earth or to Celsus's whole claim; the English keeps the Greek order and so keeps that ambiguity. 'σύγχυσις' is the LXX name of the city in Genesis 11:9 ('its name was called Confusion'), hence the citation beside 'confusion'. 'ἵνα γὰρ μηδὲν αἰνίσσηται' is concessive ('for even granting that ... speaks in no riddles'); αἰνίσσομαι means to speak in riddles, i.e. to hint at a concealed sense. εὐκαιρότερον rendered 'at a more suitable time'. τόπος taken as 'passage' (of Scripture); ἀναγωγή rendered 'higher meaning'. 'τίνες οὖν μᾶλλον τὰ τίνων παραφθείρουσιν' rendered 'Who, then, is more likely to be corrupting whose stories?', taking μᾶλλον as 'rather'; the following double question keeps the Greek present tense. The source prints 'Μω(??)σῆς' in the sentence on impartial hearers, a damaged or doubtful character in the transcription; the name is certainly Moses and is rendered so. The sons of Aloeus (Otus and Ephialtes, the Aloadae) piled mountains to reach heaven; Homer tells this (Odyssey 11.305–320), but Origen does not quote Homer, so no inline source is given. Phaethon's fire is the Greek myth Celsus compares with Sodom; no source cited. The cleansing fire and the end of the world may recall 2 Peter 3:7, 10–12, Malachi 3:2–3 and Isaiah 66:15–16, but Origen names only 'the prophets' and quotes no verse, so these stay uncited possible allusions. 'ὡς ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν' refers back to earlier arguments in this work on fulfilled prophecy. 'θεῖον πνεῦμα' capitalised as 'Spirit' because Origen means the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets; the first instance is anarthrous in Greek but 'the divine Spirit' is used both times, since English needs the article for a single, named Spirit.
